speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday of last week I proposed the following motion:
That the government cause to be brought immediately before the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, the responsible officers of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the purpose of explaining the circumstances leading to the recent affront to the premier of the province of Quebec, the response of the officers to that action and the intentions of Radio 
Canada to prevent similar future interference with free communication in publicly financed television programming.
I followed this up with a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts). I asked:
Is the minister aware of the often expressed criticism of bias in the programming of the publicly financed Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? Has he investigated the veracity of one of the reasons given by Lloyd Robertson for his recent resignation, and how does he reconcile this with this week's well publicised action of Radio Canada in Quebec?
The answer of the Secretary of State suggested that he did not understand the basic thrust of the question.
What is at issue is the integrity of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the very independence or so-called independence of which successive ministers have been boasting, or were these same ministers just looking for an excuse to get themselves off the hook? Were they looking for a means by which they could explain to the public why, though the public is financing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to the extent of over $400 million per annum, the public is to have no say through its elected representatives in just how these moneys are to be spent? The so-called independence of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is too often the answer given by the responsible ministers to stop the questioning of politicians.
Also is it wise to spend $400 million per annum for a service used by less than 10 per cent of the population? To what extent is Canadian culture influenced or affected by publicly financed programs that are not being received by an apparently indifferent population?
It was of considerable concern to me to read one of the reasons why Lloyd Robertson has moved from CBC to CTV. Union regulations restricted his reporting freedom. If we are so up-tight about political interference, should we not be equally concerned with all freedom restrictions?
It is argued by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, when it gives broad coverage to the separatist P.Q. party, that the suppression of news and the suppression of news commentary are a threat to democracy in a free society. Why then is the same freedom not accorded to those who present the news? If it was bad for Lloyd Robertson to comment on the publicly financed outlets, are we now being brainwashed by his newfound freedom on the independent network?
I will also ask to what extent the taxpayer should finance the separatist point of view, which seeks the very destruction of the institution which gives the P.Q. party its principal source of publicity? The huge salary paid to Lise Payette helps her to attempt to destroy the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as we know it today. For certain, if her party were to gain power she would not be without a job in a new Quebec government sponsored television outlet. Lise Payette is certainly a very capable performer. But then she has no worries. If she loses the election, she returns to her big salary paid by all Canadian taxpayers.

MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR EXTRA FUNDS FOR CAPE BRETON AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in reference to the questions I raised in the House yesterday concerning the rationing of Local Initiative Project funds in the constituencies of Cape Breton Island where the unemployment situation is so grave that it threatens to become destructive of human, social, and economic values. When I return to my constituency for office hours and chat with the people in the general industrial area I meet with an increasingly sad situation.
It is all right for people who enjoy the security of good government jobs or who live in a section of the country where there is a vibrant industrial base to say, "Why don't they get out of there?" The historical truth is that they have been getting out, but there are so many barriers of age, transferable skills, education, home and neighbourhood attachment that the suggestion, for all but a minority of the people there, is both impractical and, in my view, inhuman. Most of the mobility in the post-war period has been to Ontario, and it is today, and has been for several years now, hardly a place to come looking for work unless you are very well educated and specialized.
We have hopes in the long run for a new steel complex that could, if realized, turn around the economy; but in the meantime the severity of the unemployment means that short and medium term projects must be used in areas of chronic, structural unemployment. This is especially true when there are such high national levels of unemployment that are largely cyclical in nature, and enhanced by the restraint and control program, so that mobility even to the prosperous Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area is affected because of increasing unemployment there.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has recently said that he expects unemployment is going to remain at high levels up to the 1980's. Given this situation, Mr. Speaker, the government must come up with new job creation programs. This is not the place, nor do I have the time, to discuss the merits of the programs which the minister announced last Thursday and that apparently are to begin next spring. My concern now is with this winter and the severe cuts in the LIP programs in my own area and constituency. In answering my supplemental question yesterday the minister said that his information is that the formula used for the distribution of funds to the constituencies was basically the same as last year, with some modifications to ensure that the funds were directed to areas of highest unemployment.
The minister is probably now aware of the letter I wrote to him on October 8, 1976, showing that, in essence, the formula used was downplaying the amount of unemployment in my constituency by a statistical sleight of hand. His departmental representatives in Halifax, who have so heartily co-operated with me are not responsible for this but rather the blame lies
Adjournment Debate
with some of those in Ottawa who live in their ivory towers and apparently have never seen the stark, ugly reality that confronts the unemployed who no longer have UIC benefits and detest the dole.
The minister in answering yesterday the question of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) regarding the accuracy of the statistics of the labour force survey which were included in the formula, said that "we should go back to the original system of having members of parliament in the area figure out some pooling arrangement". That seems to agree with my suggestion that the minister meet with the three Cape Breton members affected and with the managers of their Manpower offices to get a more accurate picture of what is ahead this winter regarding the employment situation. I do hope he will act on this suggestion. If it is impossible for the minister to be present, he could delegate a top knowledgeable and humane official.
I do not want to have to rise in this House again this winter and ask for emergency meetings to meet the unemployment situation in Cape Breton. Last year we had three such meetings. Those meetings were attended by Manpower officials, a DREE representative, MP's and MLA's from the area, as well as Premier Regan of Nova Scotia and the president of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. The consensus of opinion was that in the long run a new steel industry was the only permanent answer to the problem. At one of those meetings it was agreed that Canada Manpower be requested to put special funds into a retraining program in the Cape Breton area to upgrade the quality of the labour force supply, both actual and potential, in the construction trades sector. The idea was that it would be a vitally important step if a new steel complex were to be initiated and become a reality with as reasonable a construction cost and timetable as would be considered possible. If the steel complex did not become a reality, then the consensus was that it would be government money well spent.
It is now near November and all we have heard from the government so far is the bad news about the serious reduction in LIP funds. I hope the minister will call the meeting referred to above on the LIP allocations soon. After all, there were over $2 million in projects applied for and I am asked to settle for $379,000 as against $810,000 last year. If the unemployment situation were to be so improved, I would indeed be a happier man, but I know the area too well and so do the Canada Manpower managers in that region, to accept that reasoning. After all, the formula is based upon last year's figures rather than current ones. We desperately need more LIP funds and special funds for the retraining mentioned above. Today's Ottawa Journal quotes the new Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) as saying he was told to "bring compassion to the job". This is an occasion for compassion and an opportunity to practice social justice also.

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member, I will say that replacement work for the aerospace industry in Canada was one of the basic conditions laid down at the beginning of the LRPA program, and the amount of industrial benefits promised at that time had a lot of importance in the choice of the Aurora aircraft by the Canadian government.
The department wanted Canadian businesses in the aerospace industry to benefit most from it. So the Lockheed Aircraft Company and Boeing were encouraged to look up all possible sources in Canada, including Nova Scotia. Two Nova Scotia firms were selected, Enheat of Amherst and IMP of Halifax, because of their excellent past performance and their

importance to their community. On representations by the minister and the department, the two companies were included in the final proposal by Lockheed as the eventual supplier of P3 components. Subject to final negotiations between the companies involved, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce expects that Enheat will produce firing domes and elevation and direction rudders for all P3 planes produced by Lockheed and not only for the Cpl40 (Aurora) while IMP will produce the electrical gear for all P3 planes and do additional work for which it is competent.
Enheat is entirely equipped to manufacture the P3 structural components and has a good reputation as far as quality, costs and delivery schedules are concerned. During the recent labour difficulties at Enheat, the department and Lockheed were naturally concerned because the time necessary to meet Lockheed's delivery schedule was running short and Nova Scotia risked losing the work by default. Therefore, official representatives of the department and Lockheed had discussions with spokesmen for the company and the government of Nova Scotia to try and speed up the settlement of that issue. In the opinion of the minister, that intervention paved the way toward bringing management and labour together in the conclusion of an agreement earlier than would have been possible otherwise.
It should be noted that IMP has no manufacturing capability but is used as a repair and overhaul base for all Argus planes. The compentence of that company is clearly in the area of repairs and overhauling.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce had great difficulty finding some manufacturing work to cover the gap left by the progressive removal of the Argus and the introduction of the Aurora and this without doubling the manufacturing capacity already existing at Enheat and in several other areas in Canada. However the electrical gear provided for IMP requires extensive manpower, a minimum of producers' goods and can be carried out with relatively unskilled personnel.
Lockheed and the department are seriously trying to find other gears or other similar works for that company, because the minister and the department feel that such a step would be beneficial to the government and the Canadian aerospace industry, contributing to maintain IMP as a very competent and productive centre of repairs and overhaul.
The comprenhensive worth of replacement works for the Aurora now under negotiation for Nova Scotia amounts to some $12 million and this figure is subject to increase during the Aurora program and could reach $17 million.
We have every reason to believe that the negotiations between Lockheed and the companies involved will soon be completed and that a contract will be awarded.

Today in Ottawa there was a representation from the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. I do not propose to discuss this issue in any detail because that will be done on another occasion, but one thing came through to me. Inconsistency in government policies affects these men very greatly especially when there are higher tariffs on the export of their product from Canada to other countries than there are on imports into Canada from those same countries. On the one hand, the government says Canada must compete in overseas markets, and on the other it makes it very difficult to compete.
The "on and off' policies of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) have a lot to do with this situation. The minister has approved certain policies which will, he says, stabilize the price paid for farm products. What he does not tell consumers is that the price will not level out at a rate equal to the average of the highs and the lows, and that the public will end up paying the higher price all the time. We have only to look at the quotas imposed on efficient producers who are told they cannot produce as much as they would like. There are boards that control the production of eggs, milk and butter. I do not know how many millions of pounds of butter or how many thousands of dozens of eggs have been spoiled as a result of this policy. The supply of turkeys and chickens is either controlled already, or will be controlled before long. I speak for the consumer because I represent a community of 80,000 consumers.
Finally I want to say I am glad that the Consumers' Association of Canada has taken up the case against some of these government policies which it realizes are not in the best interests of the public though they are in the best interests of inefficient producers. This has become evident to those who are able to make price comparisons by shopping across the line in the State of Washington, for example. It is time we reexamined the claims of the consumer and the principles involved in the implementation of the various customs tariffs.
I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) returned from Japan today. It is evident that the Japanese want to buy more raw materials from Canada. Free from the high costs and labour troubles so familiar here, Japan is readily able to produce and sell goods manufactured from the raw materials we supply. At the same time Canada as a nation wishes to manufacture and export more finished goods. Since we have the raw materials, perhaps we should control them and see to it that we do export more finished goods. Developing this proposition I would ask why Canadians should pay higher costs on imports subject to tariff, or higher costs on goods manufactured in Canada. This is not to say we want to be the hewers of wood and drawers of water we have sometimes been depicted as being. What that is to say is that the policies that have led us to the position we are now in need to be re-examined.
It is entirely possible that the people who are presently engaged in manufacturing goods that we could more cheaply buy from other countries could have their efforts diverted into

Opponents of my suggestion may say that the loss of jobs in the manufacturing industry would cause greater unemployment and ultimately be a greater burden on the taxpayer. I think that is something that could be examined. My contention would be that the net saving to the consumer would more than offset any loss that might be occasioned from greater unemployment. If, of course, the end result were greater production of goods, then on balance 1 think it would work the other way. Anyway let us not make small adjustments to, and temporary cuts in tariffs when obviously there is a deeper problem. I think it is wonderful to be a Canadian and to have Canadian industries, but I am not sure that Canadian consumers want always to be called upon to pay the very high prices that they are called upon to pay in order to support Canadian industry, and so that some consumers may work in Canadian industries.
I suggest an examination by the government might also uncover different policies that would reduce costs for the consumer. In the long run we might have better jobs for those people now employed in the manufacturing industries. In short, let us not close our eyes to deep policy examination. Let us not just patch up existing tariffs with temporary cuts or temporary anythings which are going to expire in one year, and then are extended for two, three or four years. Let us have a deep enough examination to get to the root of these problems.

At any rate the hon. member for Timiskaming said he was not in favour of extending temporary tariff cuts and mentioned two valid points, or two matters, which give businessmen much difficulty. He mentioned freight rates, which are completely beyond the control of the businessman but may affect him greatly, and referred to the customs tariff, which again is completely out of his control-the tremendous swing effects may affect particularly the small businessman who may be in difficulty through no fault of his own, owing to pressure brought to bear on the government.
The hon. member for Timiskaming also deplored the extent of government intervention in small business. I think he actually said-I mention this in case my remarks are reported to him-that he would keep government out of business. It was refreshing to hear that from a member of the NDP. I understand that party loves freedom and believes in the freedom of the individual. I certainly agree with that position. Many of our business troubles would be easier to treat if there were less government involvement with business.
When governments involve themselves in business, the inequality of treatment they mete out is one of the difficulties we encounter. It does not seem to matter which sector of the economy the government wants to help; it ends up hurting just as many, or even more people. I suppose the most recent example of the ineffectiveness of a particular government policy is the so-called peace and security package which was brought forward in the previous parliament. Before we had finished debating it at committee stage, the government itself had proposed 50 amendments to the legislation drafted under the aegis of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford).
Our customs tariff contains not a few inequities; some have been reported to the government; some I have myself reported. Unfortunately the present bill does not attempt to correct them. May I give you, Mr. Speaker, and my colleagues some examples of what I mean.
One example has to do with a hobby which interested me greatly even before I came to this place, the hobby of vintage cars. For a long time vintage car enthusiasts have been trying to persuade the government to give them relief. Those Canadians are trying to preserve part of the history of Canada, if you will, and want to restore automobiles, many of which were made in Canada. They want to keep their hobby alive in Canada. But instead of obtaining relief from the government this group of Canadians find themselves penalized at every turn. For example, they have to go to the United States to get

the old tires they need for their vehicles, and when they bring them in, the full rate of tariff is imposed on them. The same applies to the parts for these vehicles which are not manufactured in Canada. The whole history of tariffs is disregarded.
It might be said that, after all, these are automobiles and that there can be no exception for automobiles. But bear in mind that these are historic automobiles. No exception has been asked for any vehicle less than 30 years old. On the other hand the tariff does provide, in a complete about-face, that antiques-furniture and other non-mechanical things-are exempt. Anything over 100 years old is covered by the definition and is allowed into the country duty-free. The exemption applies, as well, to original works of art as long as they cost more than $20 or something like that. Any hon. members who know people who have smuggled paintings into this country can tell them they have wasted their time because they would have come in free anyway.
There is a direct relationship between original works of art and antique or vintage automobiles. Many people think of the latter as works of art and they are by definition, certainly antiques.
That is one example. The Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) gave us another today. Obviously our efforts will be in vain for many months, in any event, but in answer to questions about delay caused by people returning to Canada at the border crossing at Douglas, British Columbia, the minister indicated that more staff had been hired and, since the traffic problem seems to have been caused by Canadians returning to this country after shopping in the United States, and the fact that the groceries for which they shopped incurred duty at different rates, which involves unpacking and repacking, she would try to get the tariff changed as it affected the casual importation of groceries. I am not certain whether she intended to make it easier for Canadians by removing the duty on casual importation of groceries, or whether it was her intention to ban the casual importation of groceries, an action which would certainly have an effect in dealing with the traffic problem at the Douglas border crossing.
We find that the pressure goes on, certain businesses react to it, the business cycle is upset, and we get into more trouble than ever. There are examples I could give. Clothing manufacturers, providing jobs in Canada, have found for a variety of reasons that their operations were impracticable and they have ceased to manufacture. As a result hundreds of workers have been thrown on the job market. This is not the fault of the customs tariff, it is the fault of other government policies. The firms concerned are not going out of business. They find they can import the goods which they formerly manufactured in Canada, pay the duty, and still sell at a profit here. Jobs have been lost, but the companies stay in business by taking advantage of conflicting government policies and there is no evidence that the proposal before us has taken account of these deep-seated problems.

It is my understanding that there have been diplomatic discussions of a sensitive nature and in such cases it is up to the participants, if they so wish, to outline their role and policy.
Since Canada is a founding member of the NPT we, in conjunction with all other non-nuclear weapon state members, have IAEA safeguards applied to all of our nuclear facilities. Our position is fully consistent with the developed consensus that restricts transfers of certain equipment, materials, and technology to those countries from which we have formal governmental assurances which exclude uses which would result in the production of any nuclear explosive device. These transfers would also trigger the application of the safeguards system of the IAEA, and their retransfer to any third country could only be done on the basis of the consent of the Government of Canada.
These safeguards also apply to items covered for their useful life as well as the subsequent generation of any nuclear material which might be produced. Agreements are in place to deal with provisions for mutual concurrence on the arrangements which a recipient might wish to reprocess, store, use, transfer or retransfer any plutonium or highly enriched uranium that is covered. Standards of physical security are covered. Canadian policy is also progressive in its promotion of other international co-operative means for non-proliferation such as internationally controlled regional fuel centres.
These are policies in effect and which are shared by other supplier countries concerned about the problem. What we have seen develop is a consensus expressed in unilateral form by a number of countries to accept certain safeguard principles in all cases of nuclear exports to non-nuclear weapons states.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) that this is indeed a very important matter which the government takes very seriously, that of nuclear proliferation in the world.
It seems to me that many of the objectives outlined in clause 3 of the hon. member's bill have already been satisfied. He proposes that our exports meet the minimum criteria of the International Atomic Energy Authority. Of course that is so. Clause 3(2) refers to the re-export of spent fuel rods and would prohibit the use of fuel which has gone through a Canadian reactor to be further processed. These are the standard requirements of our export agreements at the present time under the International Atomic Energy Authority, the NPT and, of course, the nuclear suppliers group. Such objectives are applauded and encouraged by all Canadians because they naturally want to ensure that our technology, our reactors, and uranium fuel are used for peaceful purposes.
The bill proposes that we bring before parliament every agreement regarding the sale of nuclear technology, nuclear fuel, and nuclear equipment. It seems to me there would be many practical problems in doing this. Think of what is involved if every box of valves which could be used in a nuclear reactor, every agreement for the sale of every kind of equipment used in reactors, or every agreement for the sale of uranium had to be brought before parliament for consideration.
Under our traditional parliamentary practice treaties have been executed by the executive branch, the governor in council. Under our British parliamentary traditions it has not been the practice to bring treaties before parliament for ratification, such as they do in the United States and in other jurisdictions.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands suggested that the treaties which we have now, the International

Atomic Energy Agency agreement, the NPT, and the nuclear suppliers' arrangements and safeguards are completely meaningless. The hon. member is very eloquent and capable of very descriptive language, but surely he goes beyond all reason in saying that the safeguard arrangements which we have in the world are completely meaningless. Ever since the beginning of the nuclear age, Canada has been dedicated to a role of peaceful purposes for its technology, reactors, and uranium fuel.
A great deal of the public discussion continues to display a profound lack of knowledge and comprehension of the complexity of the problem of non-proliferation, of the important and far-reaching efforts deployed internationally to solve this problem effectively and of the vast progress achieved in recent years. I feel quite strongly that if this parliament, through some fault of its own were to enact the views expressed by the opposition, this could well be harmful to the active and effective pursuit of an international consensus on safeguards.
I should like to recall that during the debate on nuclear exports last March the then Secretary of State for External Affairs explained at length the pre-occupations of the government in steering a course that permits reaping the full economic benefits of nuclear power while preventing nuclear weapons' proliferation. However, I feel it important to elaborate on these issues and repeat, if necessary, some of the basic principles which have produced a Canadian safeguards policy which is the most stringent and demanding in the world today; principles which have given Canada leadership for safeguards in international meetings.
First, it must be emphasized that national and international safeguards standards have never been static. They have been in continual evolution since the first nuclear co-operation agreements were entered into in the early 1950's, and have developed steadily through innovations made by Canada and other suppliers, through elaborate and detailed consultations, and through international commitments such as the NPT and the consensus among suppliers reached at London last year. Present day levels of safeguards represent the degree of stringency which the major nuclear powers are prepared to enforce. But these are not static either. They represent a threshold from which further progress will hopefully be achieved.
The development to today's high standards has been difficult. The establishment of the International Atomic Energy Agency in 1956 was the initial step to promote multilateral safeguards regimes. At first early safeguards were primarily applied to small isolated reactors rather than to interconnected facilities. This initial system of the Agency was then further defined and extended in 1965, 1966 and 1968. Here the safeguards system was again oriented to individual facilities rather than to the fuel cycle as a whole, but each facility bears the full weight of safeguards.
Then in 1970 international consciousness had developed sufficiently to culminate in the achievement of the Non-Proliferation Treaty. Under this agreement safeguards took on specific technical objectives as opposed to the generalized statements of "peaceful purposes" which were embodied in

possible safeguards so that the people of Canada can sell a CANDU reactor in good conscience and with complete assurance that it will not be used for warlike purposes.
It is true, as the parliamentary secretary has said, that the government has attempted to impose safeguards. But in the main those safeguards are meaningless; they represent nothing more nor less than an exchange of opinion accompanied by no sanctions, no arrangements to enforce them or take retaliatory action if commitments are not kept. I believe the legislation before us would help tighten the safeguards. It is true that the only answer, ultimately, is an international agreement under the United Nations, or an international agreement signed by all the nuclear countries so that sanctions could be imposed; those who sell nuclear reactors and nuclear technology could immediately impose sanctions against any country which broke its commitments. However, if such an agreement is impossible at the present time, the legislation proposed by the hon. member for Don Valley is surely far superior to anything the government has suggested or done.
This legislation would require that any agreement signed with countries securing a nuclear reactor would involve, on their part, compliance with the latest criteria established by the International Atomic Energy Authority. I myself would go much further. I should like to see a receiving country required to sign and ratify the non-proliferation treaty.
This legislation would require that in any agreement between Canada and a purchasing country the receiving country would agree to Canada controlling the disposition of the radiation wastes-it could bring them to this country or take whatever action it wished. Moreover, the recipient country should not be able to re-export any of the nuclear technology or nuclear fuel, and would be forbidden to acquire a reprocessing plant. This is the nub of the whole question, Mr. Speaker.
Countries such as Argentina, South Korea, Pakistan-and now Brazil-have all been negotiating with France or with West Germany for the purchase of a reprocessing plant, and it has been said many times in this House that there can be no purpose whatsoever in acquiring a reprocessing plant except to extract plutonium, enabling the nation concerned to manufacture nuclear bombs.
The legislation which has been put forward forbids the purchasing country itself to construct a reprocessing plant and use the nuclear waste from the reactor. I might add that it is not difficult to construct a reprocessing plant. Scientists in India have themselves built a reprocessing plant. As the former secretary of state for external affairs admitted in the House, Argentina has already built a small reprocessing plant which it says is for experimental purposes only.
I think the most important part of this proposed bill is that it would require the government, prior to signing an agreement for the sale of a nuclear reactor, to table the documents in the House, to send the matter to a committee of the House of Commons and Senate, which must report to the House within
Ratification of Nuclear Exports 20 days so that the House would have an opportunity by vote to agree with or reject the proposed agreement.
The parliamentary secretary has put forward two objections to such an arrangement. First of all, he says that the matter of entering into treaties comes within the royal prerogative. I would remind him, first of all, that a declaration of war comes within the royal prerogative. Way back in the twenties the Right Hon. Mackenzie King himself pledged that no Liberal government would declare war on its own, that any declaration of war would have to come from parliament, and he carried out that pledge in 1939. Surely this is equally important. Such an agreement could precipitate war in some part of the world. The signing of an agreement to sell a CANDU reactor to some other country, particularly an unstable country in a troubled area of the world, is equally important and ought to be submitted to parliament.
I know the old nineteenth century argument that the executive has the right to make treaties and that, if the House of Commons does not agree, it can vote no confidence. Well, with the majority that this government has and which many governments have had and others may have in the future, that is no safeguard.
The other argument is that the voters can reject them at the next election. It will not be much protection for humanity, Mr. Speaker, after you have sold a nuclear reactor and you find the recipient has used it for warlike purposes, to ask the electorate then to deal with the government. The damage has been done.
I was amazed at the final argument that was put up by the parliamentary secretary. He said that if we had to delay the sale of a nuclear reactor until parliament dealt with the matter, it would damage our credibility and-I took down his words-"we would lose trade advantages". I repeat, Mr. Speaker, "we would lose trade advantages". If the parliamentary secretary is speaking for the government, the government should be ashamed to say that trade advantages are more important than having the elected representatives of the people given an opportunity to say whether or not Canada should place in the hands of another country the power to devastate their countryside and possibly to precipitate a nuclear war.
A nuclear war, Mr. Speaker, is not like a conventional war. Conventional wars have laid waste countries, and devastated cities. But a nuclear war has given man the capacity to destroy all life on this planet and to leave it a burnt out cinder revolving in space. Surely on a moral issue as vital as this the government is not going to refuse the elected representatives of the people a voice in determining whether or not such a formidable and important step should be taken by the Government of Canada.
I say with great seriousness to members of this House that this is not a question which should be dealt with on any political basis. I assume that members in all parts of the House have a deep social conscience as to what we as Canadians are doing with this terrible power which has been placed in our hands.

NPT to share with countries signatories to the treaty the results of its activity in the field of nuclear energy to contribute to the fast development of that form of energy, not only in developing countries but also in advanced countries whose traditional energy resources are being depleted. If our country does not meet its international commitment, it could certainly create a disenchantment concerning the NPT that could have the unfortunate effect of encouraging many countries to withdraw from the agreement while some others could abandon any plan to join.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, I shall mention the leading role played by our country in the north-south dialogue in which we try, with many countries, to find answers to get through that difficult transition period in the energy field. Since the traditional supply sources are being depleted or becoming less accessible at the same time as we are getting through a crisis caused by an unprecedented increase in oil prices, we should try to find such answers to contribute to the balance of the world economy. Nuclear energy is still a vital alternative that must play an important part in this transition period by relieving the international tension and offering a fair choice to the poorer countries. At the same time, the use of nuclear energy by advanced countries reduces the use of oil and is beneficial to developing countries which lack the resources required to be valuable competitors on the international oil market.
Mr. Speaker, those are additionnal details about our international commitments which I wanted to set out on the occasion of the introduction of Bill C-205 by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), and which I wanted to submit to the consideration of this House. These additional details complement numerous others put forward to underline the necessity to shoulder our responsibilities not only towards Parliament but also on an international level where we have a part to play and commitments to fulfil.
Mr. Speaker, as long as we do not have any worthwhile alternative to this precious source of energy that nuclear energy is, we will not be able to prevent the international community from gaining accesss to it. On the contrary, we must go on working to introduce still more efficient controls and prevent the transmission of material and equipment considered as critical. Surely this government's policy is not unalterable in matters of nuclear exports, as evidenced by some recent decisions like the end of our cooperation program with India.
My time is up, Mr. Speaker. I would have other remarks to add, but I want to give other hon. members the opportunity to express themselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of giving my wholehearted support to Bill C-205 and to commend the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) for having introduced it.

The whole question of the proliferation of nuclear weapons is not a matter which ought to be dealt with lightly. There ought to be no gamesmanship to talk this bill out so that we do not have to consider it again this session. I hope all parties will agree to give unanimous consent so that if this bill is not dealt with by six o'clock it will be set at the head of the list again in order that it may be referred to a committee of the House where it can be studied further, and from which it would be reported back to us. I make this suggestion in the belief that the matters raised in the bill before us constitute the greatest moral issue of our time.
In the past 50 years science has made more advances than were made by mankind in all the previous thousands of years in which man has inhabited this planet. The progress of science has been so rapid that social ethics and public morality have not had an opportunity to bring to bear upon the results of research the type of restraint which is necessary if man is to survive.
The two men who were the leading figures in splitting the atom, Dr. Albert Einstein and Dr. David Oppenheimer, were tremendously perturbed that this devastating power which they had placed in the hands of the people of the world might be used for destructive purposes. Thirty years ago only the United States possessed this atomic capacity. Later, the Soviet Union acquired it. As long as the two superpowers maintained a balance of terror we had some feeling of safety. Today, however, nuclear capacity has been extended to nation after nation and all the indications are that yet more nations are acquiring the capacity to produce nuclear weapons.
Canada has a major responsibility in this area because, through the work of our scientists, we have produced the CANDU reactor-and for this they deserve credit; it is probably one of the safest reactors. But it is also the reactor from which it is easiest to make use of the radiation wastes for the extraction of plutonium from which nuclear bombs can be made.
1 was surprised to hear the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Leblanc) say that only one or two countries had tricked us. That is the point of the legislation we are considering. We only need one or two countries to trick us. As a matter of fact, every time a country tricks us and uses the CANDU reactor to produce plutonium and nuclear weapons, it stimulates its neighbour to do likewise. We already have the example of India which used the reactor to produce an explosive device, a course of action which has encouraged Pakistan to do likewise. The fact that we are selling a reactor to Argentina has set Brazil in that country's footsteps. This process of proliferation is going on at an alarming rate.
The parliamentary secretary has put forward an argument which the former secretary of state for external affairs regularly advanced, namely, that Canada has a responsiblity to ensure that the scientific know-how which we have acquired is shared with less developed countries. I believe we do have such a responsibility but I claim equally that the developing countries also have a responsibility, which is to accept the tightest
October 26, 1976

ments we are negotiating with other countries. Such a process would jeopardize not only our international credibility but also the resulting commercial advantages of such a sale, treaty or contract.
In this field, as in many others, the executive power must be able to assume its responsibilities by retaining the initiative of its negotiations with regard to nuclear exports. Needless to say, that initiative is conditional upon certain criteria which, in the last few years, as all hon. members know, the present government made it its duty to elaborate with a view to preventing the proliferation of nuclear arms, which threat must command the utmost awareness and which, because of the importance it is given, on a daily basis must hold the complete attention of those who are responsible for formulating that policy.
Indeed, because we are aware of the extreme importance we must give our nuclear policy, the former Minister of External Affairs, the Hon. Allan MacEachen, endeavoured to explain to the House, during the debate on March 23 last, the guidelines of our policy as well as its inherent characteristics.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to refer to that debate since it gives an account, in clear and specific terms, of just how concerned this government is about checking the proliferation of nuclear arms while allowing those developing countries, that have the infrastructure and the guarantees of security required for cooperative agreements in that field, to have access to the technology we are in a position to supply them. I have no intention of reviewing the agreements put forward over the years in this regard, but I would like to remind you that the government has the duty of assuming its responsibilities in such a way as to make sure that we participate actively in the economic development of those countries-those with which we deal-while at the same time respecting our international responsibilities to avoid nuclear arms proliferation. It is certainly not by staying aside and burying our heads in the sand that we will finally help efficiently reduce nuclear proliferation after considerable investments were made to develop a nuclear technology which, despite its risks, solves, in an adequate and economical way, the crucial problems we are facing.
We must pursue our endeavours to establish additional mechanisms to ensure the peaceful use of this new source of energy, and I think the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) raised the problem with Bill C-205 because it seems that occasionally some countries do not always make a peaceful use of the products we export, in opposition to the agreements we made with them.
I suggest that it is a challenge we have to take up, which the present government did with great success-I say this in spite of the little experience I have gathered in this area up to date, I must confess-since our nuclear technology remains accessible to those who express a legitimate need to purchase it and the will to accept some safeguards and conditions which rule out any possibility of nuclear explosion or other forbidden uses. It is because we are convinced that the NPT is still the
Ratification of Nuclear Exports best way to fight against nuclear proliferation that we decided to be more active, in order to complete the adherence to the treaty of the fifteen-odd la'rger countries which are not yet signatories to it.
An eventual decision by Canada to end its sales of nuclear reactors would surely remove a major factor in the foreign policy of Canada at a time when our country is considered as playing an active role in such a delicate sector. We will never insist enough on the fact that proliferation can be prevented or at least reduced as a long term danger only through coordinated and constant action by the various supplier countries and their customers. We must realize that we are not the only country which supplies nuclear materials and we do not have all the customers in the world; other countries are clients or suppliers.
Now unless there is complete and total agreement among all those countries, it is rather difficult, as I said, to reduce the long term danger. Withdrawal of Canada from the international market would only remove the influence and the role which we have played up to now not only in restricting the danger of proliferation but also in being party to drafting more effective international safeguards. It is with that mind that Canada has lately made increased efforts to set more rigorous standards in such key sectors as reprocessing, recycling, storing, selling or reselling plutonium as well as enriched uranium. Nobody ignores that as a country exporting nuclear reactors Canada has been in a position up to now to contribute to the development of solutions in those sectors, which solutions have gone a long way, in my opinion, toward clarifying the situation and lessening international stress.
I am quite delighted in that respect at the recent statements of France's Higher Council for Foreign Nuclear Policy and at the indications given in American newspapers as to the future direction of the American nuclear policy which show more restrictive policy as far as exports are concerned while insisting on the necessity of a common and coordinated rather than unilateral approach to the problems of proliferation. Of course we are encouraged by these signs which are, in several cases, similar to criteria already included in the Canadian nuclear policy and which are consistent with principles of the utmost importance for us in Canada.
Such an initiative in countries among the more active in the nuclear field can only encourage us to continue our action. On the other side, we can only recall that on another occasion, the adoption of much stricter safeguards in the nuclear policy endorsed by the government in December 74, our action was also exemplary since it encouraged the group of supplier countries known as the London Club to adopt guidelines similar to ours in 1975. During the same period we have witnessed the development of existing international consultation mechanisms and a greater cooperation to encourage supplier countries to control more efficiently their radioactive material reprocessing plants by looking for practical arrangements concerning the management of plutonium.
I shall also remind hon. members that Canada has also committed itself, according to the terms of clause 4.2 of the

In addition, the bill requires that all safeguard agreements be permanent and, most importantly, that every safeguard agreement signed by the government of Canada comes to parliament for ratification before it is signed. Any proposed agreement would have to be submitted 25 sitting days before the intended date of signature to a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate. That committee would have to report back to the House, and within 20 days that agreement would have to be called for debate in the House, and within five days after being called it would have to be put to a vote.
Surely, it is the responsibility of every member of parliament to be concerned about this matter. Surely, it is common sense for something which is so important to the future of mankind to be debated in our House of Commons. Even in the United States, where there is a complete separation of the legislative and administrative functions, legislation has been passed so that there has to be positive affirmation on the part of Congress before there can be an export of nuclear technology. Surely, we cannot accept the proposition that we must make this nuclear technology available to less developed countries immediately in order to help their development. It defies logic to suggest that it is more important for an underdeveloped country to have a nuclear potentiality today-even though we do not have the necessary safeguards-than it is to wait until such safeguards can be developed in an effective fashion. Indeed, the argument that we are only selling to less developed countries is strange in the extreme when we talk about exporting to Japan and had negotiations with Iran about nuclear reactors.
It is argued that if we do not make nuclear technology available, other countries will. But surely that cannot be the issue. On something as important as the risk of weapons being developed by other countries, we cannot decide the issue on the basis of commercial considerations. It is a moral question. All that Canada brings to the field of international negotiations is its moral position and surely Canada has the moral responsibility of slowing down the possible spread of nuclear weaponry.
If one wants to use the commercial argument, there is need for power development in this country. We can use all the nuclear reactors we can build and all the heavy water we can produce domestically. However, aside from that, it is wrong for Canada to be involved in the export of nuclear reactors when we know that the product of reactors can be used- because it has been used in India-for the development of atomic weapons.
I urge everyone in this House to allow this bill to go forward-and not to talk it out-so that years from now every member of parliament can say that when he or she was called on the issue of what Canada should do about the spread of nuclear potentiality, he or she had an opportunity in the House of Commons or in the Senate to vote on it.

Mr. Speaker, I must say first of all that it is the first time that I have the honour and the pleasure, since my appointment as Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to take part in a debate in this House about the responsibilities of that department. I also wish to commend the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) for introducing Bill C-205. Of course, I agree with many points raised by the hon. member who took it upon him self to introduce such an important bill.
However, before taking a definite stand on the bill, I do not think we should, as a government, impute motives to those countries we deal with in that area. It may have happened on one or two occasions that some countries played dirty tricks on us following a sale. But I do not think that principle applies generally to all the countries we deal with. I feel it is also important, Mr. Speaker, to remind this House of a few highlights of the Canadian nuclear policy and to express my views on the constitutional question as to the necessity of securing parliamentary ratification, and I refer to section 5 of Bill C-205, for the export of nuclear fuels, equipment and technology.
As hon. members know, it is not customary for this House to seek parliamentary approval in order to ratify a treaty or to commit this country through international agreement or treaty. In Canada, and the hon. member for Don Valley knows it better than I do, the constitutional authority to enter into arrangements such as treaties is part of the royal prerogative commonly exercised by the governor in council. Such ratification is therefore incumbent upon the executive. However, this government has always made it a point, and I want to emphasize this, to distribute to the hon. members any important documents related to nuclear exports. that Bill C-205, respecting the parliamentary ratification of the export abroad of nuclear fuels, equipment and technology, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think everyone on all sides of the House of Commons would agree that there is no more pressing matter facing all mankind than the capability of various nations to develop nuclear weaponry which has the capacity of destroying all mankind. The existence of this capability has grown tremendously during the last two decades. Immediately and for a decade after world war II only a few nations possessed the capability of destroying the world with nuclear bombs, and the balance of power at that time made the possibility of such destruction taking place reasonably slight, but today, as the Stockholm Peace Institute has reported, 35 countries will have nuclear weaponry by 1985. The institute reports, further, that with 35 countries having the capability of
Ratification of Nuclear Exports exploding nuclear weapons, the possibility of maintaining peace, and indeed the world, until the end of the twentieth century is slight indeed.
It seems to me that it is unfortunate that Canada has become one of the nations which is in the forefront of the spread of nuclear technology throughout the world by pressing the sale of our nuclear reactors to various countries. We know all too well what happens when we sell these nuclear materials without appropriate safeguards. In our sale of nuclear devices we have been, essentially, double-crossed by India, which is now one of the dictatorships of the world. We know that unless there are appropriate safeguards it is almost certain that some of our nuclear reactors will be used for other than peaceful purposes.
1 was astonished to read in the newspapers today that it is hoped that one of the things which will come out of the trip of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to Japan is an opportunity to sell more nuclear reactors to that country and to thereby contribute to the possibility of power struggles in the Far East. We have supplied a reactor to Argentina, one of the most unstable countries in the world, and while I want to debate this point as a moral issue and not as a commercial one, it is interesting to note that we not only supplied a reactor to Argentina but we did it at enormous cost to Canadian taxpayers. We are supplying reactors to Korea, a country which spends more dollars per capita on weaponry than any other country in the world. We know that the safeguards on the export of nuclear technology are not adequate. In the report issued by the Atomic Energy Commission it is stated that the safeguards are not adequate at the present time. Therefore, it seems to me to be common sense, if nothing else, that every member of parliament should be concerned about what has to be one of the most important issues in the world today.
The bill I introduced, and for which I ask the support of all hon. members, proposes-and I do not see how anyone can oppose this-that Canada not sell nuclear devices, as defined in the bill, nuclear reactors, technology and fuels, to any country which does not sign the safeguards agreement of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Second, the bill calls for the return, if appropriate, of spent fuel from the reactors to Canada. This is the only true safeguard in the control of the use of nuclear reactors at the present time. The bill would forbid the re-export of any technology, equipment or fuel from a country which buys them from us, and it would prohibit the importing country which buys a nuclear reactor from us from acquiring a reprocessing plant, so that it cannot take the material which comes from our reactors and reprocess it into a fuel which can be used for a weapon.
One of the issues of debate today is the fact that France is trying to sell to Pakistan a reprocessing plant. There is no reason in the world for any country to buy a reprocessing plant if it does not want to get involved in the weaponry business. That is what a reprocessing plant is all about. We should not allow our reactors to go to a country in which there is any possibility that a reprocessing plant will be acquired.

Some comments have been made this afternoon by various members who have preceded me on the question of perhaps never needing tariffs, the controversy of free trade versus fair trade. I should like to think that in many instances we do not want tariff protection, and shortly 1 will dwell on a few of those instances. But in fact industry in Canada is about one-tenth the size of industry in the United States, obviously because the population, the community to which we sell our goods, is one-tenth the size of that in the United States. Unfortunately, however, in many of the industries, and a few in my own riding, the unions have brought the rates and the benefits which they are claiming up to well above their U.S. counterparts. As a consequence, their ability to compete is drastically hindered.
I should like to make a point regarding the small community in the southeast portion of my riding which until about two years ago had produced a very fine product. They sold it in Canada reasonably competitively, but when the market in this product depressed in the United States, the major American producers merely had to slough off about 10 per cent of the surplus production to completely dominate the Canadian market at a price with which the Canadian producer in my riding could not compete. There was no protection. This factory was particularly efficient for its size. It was relatively new, it turned out a good product; but without protection it was unable to compete in the depressed market.
The effect of taking away some 325 jobs in a small community of about 1,500 souls in total was devastating. It has been quite a while since we have had such a blow. But the federal government would not protect the industry, and when the industry finally closed its doors and people were out of work, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion would not assist in any way because they said unemployment was not high enough. I do not know how high it has to go in a small community before they are prepared to intervene.
Let me say, in passing-and I am not in particular trying to blow my own horn-that we were successful. I was instrumental in bringing a new industry to the vacant factory. They are not going to have as many men as were there before. This new industry is part of a large international industry. They will be able to compete. The government of Ontario saw fit to help them with $500,000-but, once again, DREE was not prepared to help. Fortunately, their product is one which comes under the auto pact and they will not need the tariff protection which the previous tenants had. The only help we got from the federal government is that which you get when you start any plant under Canada Manpower in support of the initial salaries of employees.
The problem of getting a plant like that started brings up another point to which 1 would like briefly to refer in passing. In the throne speech, a great to-do was made about the Federal Business Development Bank. It is the same thing as the Industrial Development Bank, the same bird, the same feathers-and, frankly, it will produce the same kind of fertilizer as the IDB. With their usurious rates, their unreasonable

collateral requirements, and their shameless loss record, they do nothing to encourage Canadian industry. A few years ago I spent a good deal of time going into that matter in some detail, and I do not intend to do so now.
Closer to my own home, right in the city in which I live, is an industry that for many years has been competitive in the market. About two years ago they brought to my attention a problem they were having with the Department of Finance. They pointed out that one of the major products which they use could be brought in from France and Italy at a lower price than they could produce the product in Belleville, simply because of the taxes that were applied to the product made in the Belleville plant. I took this matter up with the then minister of finance and, suffice it to say, since then I have a file many inches thick. In effect, the department has acknowledged that there is a problem and that sooner or later they will do something about it. I hope they will do it soon because that plant has announced they are closing their doors, which they will do in December of this year, at which time they will lay off some hundreds of employees. They will start to package their product in a much smaller warehousing operation in Belleville.
While it is not entirely the result of this tax problem, in my opinion the correcting of the tax problem expeditiously would have prevented them from taking action for the time being. Once again, in 1967-68 they were assisted by the provincial government when they were having some problems, and they fulfilled their responsibilities to the provincial government and were kept running for another seven or eight years. That extra employment in a small community the size of Belleville, which numbers some 35,000 people, is worth-while.
These are some of the things that the new minister faces. Since I have left ten more minutes of my time, Mr. Speaker, and it is nearly five o'clock, I would like to call it five o'clock and continue after dinner.

Can we expect to have higher wages and take this money out of the economy and buy our food more cheaply across the border? Surely people will do this. People are built this way, and this is what they will do.
The government, however, has an obligation. It was here when the situation was created. The government allowed this to happen and has an obligation to do something about it. The fruit farmers in the Okanagan tell me that they can grow fruit as cheaply as anyone. They have to pay more for spray. They go across the border and bring it in, in order to become competitive.

The producers in Washington state, in the United States, use pretty well the same water we use, except that we must pay more for it because we have had the expense of putting in the dams and the systems to hold it back in the hills, and they pick it up when it is down in the mainstream. Because of this, the Americans do not have the same expense that we have. We can go across the line and bring in equipment duty-free, if someone will sell it to us. We need healthy farm, textile and manufacturing industries in Canada in order to create jobs for Canadians. Let the market go to work and let the manufacturers go to work creating jobs. Mr. Speaker, I, also, intend to intervene briefly in respect of Bill C-15, the Customs Tariff bill. I will attempt to limit my remarks so that I can close by five o'clock. At the outset I should like to take the opportunity, because I did not speak in the throne speech debate, to publicly express my congratulations to you, sir, in your new position. We will look forward to your wisdom and guidance from the chair, and I am confident that all members will respect your judgment.
Tariffs can usually be equated with protection. Had I spoken on the throne speech, I would have spent most of the time talking about the problems of small industry and other production facilities in the Hastings area which are in difficulty. This bill, however, gives me a much better platform from which to express these views. Also, had I spoken in the throne speech debate I would have had a few words to say about some of the members of the cabinet. I will, for the most part, limit my thoughts to the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) who has been appointed Secretary of State for some ambiguous purpose of assisting small industry.
It is very commendable that all of a sudden the government has realized that small industry has a place in Canada and that the people who work in small industry are taxpayers who would benefit from a strong, industrial community in Canada. 1 believe, however, that the minister will end up having the sympathy of most members of the House because, frankly, I am not at all sure what it is he is to do. True enough, the throne speech devoted a whole paragraph to the high regard in which the government holds small industry, it seems that the minister will be doing quite a bit of travelling. He is already on his way to Russia. Frankly, I do not think he will sell much over there. I am not sure what they could teach us in the way of free enterprise. In his new position, I think the new minister should attempt to obtain some co-operation. It seems to me he could co-ordinate some of the awkward functions of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Revenue, the Department of Regional Economic Affairs, and last, but nof least, certainly the Department of Finance. If he did this, he would really be doing something.

asked what we expected to trade to Japan, what they needed from us, the answer was, "CANDU reactors and STOL aircraft". I do not think we need to trade-off our natural resources in this manner. I do not think the Canadian people believe we have to, either. We do not have to be soft in our trading with other countries which need our natural resources. It is because they are necessities to they them that we can be hard.
Duties and tariff policies in Canada have not kept pace with inflationary tendencies, and to further aggravate the problem there have been two duty reductions in the past four years on virtually all food items. Let me put on the record some examples of Canada's cheap food policy. In 1975 this country imported 83 per cent more dairy products than in 1973. Likewise, in 1975 Canada imported 370 per cent more berries than in 1973. Some 58 per cent more apples were imported in 1975 than in 1973, 200 per cent more honey, 74 per cent more jams, 294 per cent more chicken, 33 per cent more canned ham, and 1,086 per cent more tobacco, though only a few us eat tobacco.
In 1974, Canada imported five million pounds of chicken from the United States, which amounted to less than one-tenth of 1 per cent of Canadian production. In the same year, 1974, this country exported 12 million pounds of chicken to Cuba. However, in 1975 Canada had literally no exports of chicken-so hon. members can see just how fast we were kicked out of Cuba. Nevertheless, we imported over 12 million pounds from the United States, making an increase of nearly 250 per cent in the import figure. This year the trend has continued at an ever faster rate. Figures up to June, 1976, show that Canada has imported 22 million pounds of chicken from the United States. Year-end imports are estimated to be 50 million pounds, up 400 per cent over 1975 and equalling 7 per cent of Canada's total production.
This is the sort of thing being experienced by Canadian food processors today, Mr. Speaker. Food processors and canners in Canada are in very dire, desperate straits. They are going out of business because they cannot compete with imports of canned, processed products from other parts of the world. Last year, the big canning companies and some of the big chain stores sent their labels to Australia and the United States to be put on canned goods in those countries and sent back to Canada.
As far as the manufacturing was concerned, the only job that we in Canada got was the labels. Possibly that was because of the bilingual requirement on labels. That could not be done there, so it was necessary to have it done here. Just think of the number of people in Canada being put out of work as a result of this. What is happening in the farm production area? This is the trend in Canada today. This government must accept responsibility for this trend. They have made it very easy to do this kind of thing. There is no real farm policy or food policy, only a cheap food policy. When these companies go out of business, we will be subject to the whims of

other countries. We do not have the kinds of policies that would do anything in the event of a national emergency.
Fresh fruit and vegetables are another example of the bad position that producers are in across Canada. There are unnatural barriers in these areas as far as tariffs are concerned. Transportation cost on fruit coming from the Okanagan Valley to eastern Canada are as much as one cent a pound higher than the rates being paid by United States competitors. They have this one-cent a pound advantage even though part of their shipping is done on Canadian railroads. When the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) visited that area about a month ago, the producers asked him about this and the minister replied that if they could ship cheaper on American railways, that was the way they should do it. I submit that that is not a very good way for this government to be talking to producers in Canada.
Stripped potatoes coming into British Columbia have been affecting potato prices. These potatoes are stripped off crops in the United States. They are not put on the American market because that would upset their market price. Instead, they are sent to Canada, upsetting our market price. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was asked about this. He replied that the government would stabilize prices. Our producers want to operate on a competitive basis. They do not want stabilization. However, they have had to accept stabilization because they do not get anything else from this government. Because of the cheap food policy, the producers must accept large hand-outs from the government. I wonder whether Canadians would not pay the price rather than have their tax dollars go toward stabilization. How long can we operate in this way?
It is time that we took a serious look at the automatic surcharge. This has been used in Canada before, but we seem to be araid of it. I believe the automatic surcharge would stop this kind of situation. When we stop to take a good look at the situation, we see that the consumer does not benefit. The consumer does not get the product any cheaper. The one who gets it cheaper is the person who brings it into Canada. By the time the consumer gets it, it is the same price as the top Canadian product. With these cheaper imports, the Canadian producer cannot sell without cutting his price down to that of the import price. However, the price to the consumer does not change. There are many examples of this. One occurred here in Ottawa last year. Even though the consumer had to pay a good price for apples, the producer received very little. This is what happens in the marketing system.
Stabilization is open to many abuses. All the producer wants is to get his money from the marketplace. Early last spring 1 asked the minister about Canadian apple producers having to pay higher transportation costs than their competitors in the United States. I pointed out that this was a trade barrier. The minister replied that if we could prove that, he would provide stabilization. Well, it was not hard to prove. Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to talk on the Customs Tariff bill. I should like to express my appreciation of the eloquent speech delivered by my hon. friend from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) on this subject. He set the tone for the debate which should be carried on with respect to this subject.
These are times in which many Canadian industries are facing serious hardship. The minister maintained, in the course of his speech, that the Customs Tariff left room for accommodation in cases of genuine hardship. But although we know that a lot of hardship is being experienced, we cannot find any use being made of this leeway, or whatever the minister had in mind. At the present time, a serious situation faces those engaged in the manufacture of textiles, shoes, mobile homes, boats, farm products, electronics and a number of other commodities.
I read in the newspaper the other day that the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) was calling for a federal inquiry into the price of food in British Columbia. The hon. member for Windsor West was minister of consumer and corporate affairs at one time, and I would remind the House that this is a situation which has been developing over many years; it did not arise overnight. Moreover, it is not confined to British Columbia. I wonder why he is not calling for a federal inquiry into prices across Canada generally, including the price of hardware, chemicals and equipment where the cost of importation appears to be disproportionately high.
Let me take, as an example, the sprays we use in orchards in British Columbia. These are manufactured in the United States; they come up through the valleys of Washington into the valleys of British Columbia, and they are duty-free. A year ago it was impossible to buy them without paying 30 or 40 per cent more than the price just across the border. In other words, the border crossing, without duty, raised the price by between 30 and 40 per cent. This is not a tariff barrier, Mr. Speaker; it is a border barrier, one which is manufactured, nobody knows why. I know this to be the case because fruit growers in my area were crossing the line to buy their sprays in the United States: it was the only thing they could do if they were to remain competitive with fruit growers in that country.
Some might say that a situation of this kind is not the responsibility of the federal government. In my opinion, it is. Why does this sort of thing happen? Situations of this kind need to be investigated, as well as the high price of food, and I hope the hon. member for Windsor West will urge the govern-
Customs Tariff
ment to broaden the inquiry he proposes and extend it to other areas. Indeed, he should have taken action along these lines when he was minister of consumer and corporate affairs.
As far as imports into Canada are concerned, the two industries most seriously affected are farming and textiles. Canada is the only country in the world which fails to protect farm products. We are aware of the great outcry among Canadians in favour of preserving our farmlands, the general feeling that no more of it should be paved over or otherwise destroyed. Yet that has been the response of government, especially the federal government? We are the only country in the world that does not protect farm products. How can we have one without the other? Many other countries of the world have goals for food production which are intended to maintain the level of production and guarantee a reasonable supply of a particular commodity in times of international emergency. We do not have any such thing and are trying to preserve farmland.
Other countries have tariffs and quotas and they also have trade barriers. I think the worst of these is the trade barrier. The hon. member for Timiskaming said that we should not close our border and make it easy to create a situation where we accommodate companies and industries that are not competitive and efficient. I agree with that. I do not think anyone is asking that our borders be closed so that we can accommodate inefficient industries, but what we do want is the same kind of deal that other countries have.
As far as trade barriers are concerned, I have made reference to a certain spray which is manufactured by another country. This is the sort of thing that happens in Canada, yet our government sits idly by and does absolutely nothing about it. Other countries have quotas to protect their farming industry. If their farming industry becomes endangered, they erect trade barriers, just as the Japanese have done against apples from British Columbia. They say these apples have codling moth and therefore they cannot accept them. We have proved beyond a shadow of doubt that their apples also have it, but it does not matter; they do not want our apples anyway. That is the kind of trade barrier they have erected. We do not do this sort of thing. Canada can rightly be described as a saint in a world of sinners. I say, let us have free trade. I think most Canadians are not against free trade so long as it is fair trade.
The hon. member for Timiskaming also said that if we had free trade in this world we could produce, manufacture and compete. I believe that is very much the case, but we cannot do so under the structure we have in the world today. We do not have fair trade, yet we are calling for free trade. Under this guise of free trade, Canada has a cheap food policy. We trade-off our raw materials and natural resources with another country in return for food and textiles, the basic commodities that we have in Canada. That is the kind of trade-back we get on almost every occasion when we want to sell a CANDU reactor or a STOL aircraft. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been in Japan on a trade mission, and when it was
