schedules and rates are established and say, "These rates are sacred." It is almost as if the tariff structure were the unchanging Bible or Talmud of the Tariff Board.
I wish the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) would involve himself less with agriculture. It has been said that we turn to the Minister of Finance when the agricultural industry is in difficulty. I think international agriculture would be a lot better off if governments stayed out of the field, and I mean provincial, federal and other governments. All over the world governments are involved with agriculture. All over the world governments pay subsidies to agriculture. Every time a subsidy is paid, or one country's tariff is adjusted, the effects are felt in all other countries.
I agree with the Minister of Agriculture that, whether we like it or not, we are dealing in an international market and are affected by it. What the Australians do with their beef affects the market in the United States, Canada and even the Common Market. Beef sales affect the sale of pork, eggs and other protein foods. Therefore, changes in one part of the world in one commodity affect markets in many other countries in that same field. Yet it is difficult to make changes; and changes, even when needed, are slow in coming. The Egg Marketing Board, previously mentioned, contends that it has the right to limit the number of eggs coming into the country. I think they should have that right. Before they can exercise it, they must go to the Minister of Finance. He must allow the required time to go by before acting, consult people in the field, check with the interested people in GATT and then introduce changes. But the effect of such changes may be detrimental, not advantageous. It seems to me that such action is not really what we need. If we are to compete with other countries we must process more of our raw materials in labour-intensive industries.
Mr. Speaker, factories in the area I represent deal probably with every country of the world. They export diamond drilling equipment and diamond drill-bits to almost every mining venture in the world. It has not been easy for them to compete. Whenever a new development, new process or new piece of machinery is introduced, they immediately run up against our entire tariff structure. They have survived because they are probably more competent than others in the field anywhere in the world. My point is this: we must increase our capacity for employing people, because many of the commodities we used to export from this country are no longer abundantly available.
It was easy to run up a favourable balance of trade when you could export oil as if it were going out of style, or ship out in a totally unprocessed state this country's mineral wealth. Now, many commodities are in short supply. We now know that we do not possess endless resources of coal, oil, iron ore as well as other basic commodities. Therefore, we must process these commodities in this country and make sure we do it in a way which will allow us to compete.
If we lived in a world of free trade, a world in which governments did not intervene in the market, I am sure that we could, to our great advantage, trade with other countries around the world. Unfortunately, we do not live in such a

world. We have earned money with raw material exports, but have spent large sums in subsidizing commodities exported.
Let me give an example, Mr. Speaker. We, in northern Ontario, a few years ago were shipping iron pellets to Pittsburgh. It cost us 2'A times as much to ship the iron out as it did to bring in the clay necessary for making those pellets. Why did this happen? The Ontario government owned the railway serving the area and heavily subsidized the goods going out. 1 did not subsidize anything coming in. If we are to compete, we must do better than this. Too many road-blocks have been thrown up by governments. If we are to compete, we must tear them down. I related the example of the glue. Mr. Speaker, in that case the company hired an expert consultant from Germany. He had been the consultant to almost every plant on the North American continent built to make that kind of product. But our Tariff Board was not sympathetic. It said that we would eventually be able to develop that kind of glue in this country; therefore, the tariff on it would not be removed. That tariff added considerable cost to the finished product and made it harder for companies using the glue to remain competitive.
This story has been repeated in other areas. For example, in my area a manufacturer wanted to erect a plant in which he could assemble stoves prefabricated in the United States. The stoves were to be sent to my area; they were not built in Canada, Mr. Speaker. Yet the tariff cannot be removed because, they say, another stove manufacturing company possesses a number of patents in the same field and maybe intends to manufacture that commodity.
In my view, the tariff structure of this country has not been advantageous to the small manufacturer. Looking down the list, I find myself wondering whether the minister can explain why the tax is 35 per cent in some cases and 10 per cent or 5 per cent in others. Take, for example, preparations of cocoa and chocolate in powdered form. Mr. Speaker, I agree with the previous speaker that our economy is not strong and it is not getting much stronger. I disagree, however, with his contention that we can solve this problem with additional changes to the Customs Tariff arrangements. I was not able to ascertain whether he favoured a closed market or an open market, but I agree that for years we have played with this Customs Tariff question. It may turn out to be the deciding factor in what happens to our developing industries in Canada.
Customs Tariff
I also agree with him that we must develop a more labourintensive industrial strategy for the country, but if it is not developed on a sound basis we will be in serious trouble. We must realize the dangers of closing off our border and providing the kind of protection that would allow the development of inefficient domestic industries. In the end, the cost would be greater than the advantages.
In the years that I have been a member of parliament it has become apparent to me that there are two areas of the Canadian economy of which members have no knowledge and over which we have no control. The first of these is freight rates. It has been said that in order to do anything about freight rates we would have to bring an expert in from the United States because we do not have anyone who understands the tariff and freight structure involved in moving goods about this country.
The second area is the Customs Tariff. Of the thousands and thousands of tariffs we have, it seems to me that any changes made to them are almost entirely made at the wish of the civil servants who administer them. I shall cite an example from my constituency, Mr. Speaker. A small, innovative company holds patents on a number of processes in its field and qualified for a DREE grant. As an aside, I received an invitation from the patent office to a celebration on the issue of the millionth patent in this country. Some of these patents have been valuable and show our ability to develop industrial processes and items.
Going to the Tariff Board is something like going to China, Mr. Speaker: 1 choose China because I do not understand anything about its character structure or language, and our tariff structure is something like that. This company asked for the removal of duty on a certain kind of glue imported from the United States. The Tariff Board sought outside opinion and eventually turned down the application because Shell claimed they knew how to make the glue and would make it some time in the future. Because it might be made in Canada in future, the duty could not be removed. The glue is an expensive part of the covering used on flake-board in this country. Interestingly, some companies were buying the flake-board from manufacturers in Portland, Oregon, and shipping the finished product to major television and stereo manufacturers in New York. But the Tariff Board could not see merit in reducing or removing the tariffs which drove up the price of this product. Consequently, the particular company of which I am thinking made less money and was less competitive than similar companies making the finished product in other countries. This sort of thing happens all the time.
Who will correct the situation? Nobody will, apparently. Nobody, including the minister, will talk to the people on the Tariff Board. The minister is a smart man; he has learned another language, but I do not think he can talk in tariffese, or whatever you may call the language spoken by the people on the Tariff Board. They do not understand the problem. They merely look at the thousands of commodities for which

One can be as cute as one wants in non-tariff barriers: it is like punching a pillow. Therefore, it is quite easy for these various countries to impose quotas or introduce non-tariff barriers, and Canada does it, too. We negotiate quota restrictions with, shall we say, a big club. In the field of quota restrictions on textiles we are acting like every other country in the word. There is not a country in the world which does not protect its textile industry. The only industry which usually gets greater protection is the agricultural industry, and here in Canada that is certainly the case. My colleagues will tell us just how far we go to protect our agricultural industry. It is not a matter of whether the tariff is high or low; it is a question of whether there is actually a national food policy.
It may be suggested that I am straying some distance from the Customs Tariff, but I am not. Second reading, particularly of a bill to amend the Customs Tariff, is the appropriate time to discuss whether there should be a continued reduction of rates or a temporary increase which may become a permanent increase; whether there should be quota restrictions, which have been resorted to by the Minister of Agriculture with regard to meat; or whether there should be quota restrictions which are negotiated with a number of third world countries with regard to synthetic textiles.
In outlining the problem, I am not going to say that I have a solution, but there is a situation with regard to Canadian manufacturers and Canadian supplier and it is the responsibility of the government to respond. But there has been a deafening silence from the ranks of the government. It is no answer to ask what we should do. Hon. members opposite have prided themselves on the fact that the Canadian people have put their confidence in them. Well, let them assume their responsibilities. Liberal governments have been in office now for 13 years and the problem of trade imbalances on the commodity side has been ever present. There has been the odd year when there has been a trade surplus, but those where the years when we were exporting petroleum, natural gas, iron ore and semi-processed nickel in vast and increasing quantities.
The Liberals have been the ones who have created the big surplus on the commodities side, but let us deal with labourintensive commodities. Let us deal with Canadians in small towns. It is not big cities like Toronto, Montreal, Edmonton, Vancouver, Winnipeg, Calgary or Hamilton which face the major problems. I invite hon. members, particularly hon. members from the province of Quebec and from small communities in Ontario, to tell us at great length the difficulties occasioned by the closing of this plant or that business employing 60 to 100 employees. These are things which knock the heart out of those communities.
We are at the core of these problems, but how do we handle them? Should the answer be to offer palliatives? Is the answer to offer grants? Is the answer to keep pumping hundreds of

millions of dollars through a DREE program, which is just like putting sand into a sack which is full of holes? What good does it do to pump into a town a few hundred thousands dollars to, so to speak, rehabilitate a business or establish a business which goes out of operation in three years time? There has to be a much more fundamental attack on the problem. We can have the best commodities, the best machinery, the best clothes and the best shoes, but if we cannot sell them either abroad or at home we cannot build enough shelves upon which to store them and we do not have enough money to finance all that inventory.
I challenge hon. members to listen not only to other hon. members in this House but also to other Canadians who are equally concerned about this problem. Let us hear from newspaper editors who are all too ready to provide quick solutions and advice. Let us hear from academics in universities who are also quick to tell parliament, and particularly the government, how to do its business. All Canadians must participate in solving this problem.
We have been caught up in a fight against inflation. In budget debates going back to the early 1970s, and even before, I and my colleagues have spoken about the dangers of inflation and how it was a real cancer which has rooted into the Canadian economic body. Thank goodness I have the speeches on record; it is not a matter of merely saying, "I told you so". Our warnings were brushed aside and pooh-poohed. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that we lived in the best of all possible worlds. Where are we today? We have gone through a violent spasm with regard to inflation, and we are not over it by a long shot.
In addition to inflation we have an unemployment problem. I would like to hear suggestions from members of the New Democratic Party and others who profess a professional interest in unemployment other than raking leaves. We can all rake leaves at minimum wages, but we get nowhere. One can say that investment can be directed to produce anything, but unless those goods and services which are produced are bought, and unless they are produced at economic and competitive prices, the whole exercise is a sham and a hypocrisy. We want to hear about solutions now. I ask hon. members to offer suggestions, because centred on these tariff changes we are looking at problems of international trade. Let us remember that international trade is not just selling goods abroad.
There is another item with regard to international trade, and that is the matter of imports. I referred to people in the lower mainland of British Columbia driving across the border to buy their groceries. I am sure that the same is being done in the Windsor-Detroit area and everywhere along the United States border where there are major shopping areas close by. There is presently a constant drive by Canadians to buy on the other side of the border at worth-while prices. That is lost business; it is all imports. Maybe it is a good thing to be able to buy Dare biscuits manufactured in Surrey, British Columbia, at 20 cents per pound cheaper in Bellingham, Washington, but I think it is a problem that we have to tackle.

There is duty on certain groceries coming back to Canada, but on a $70 purchase it is about $1.50, when already $20 to $25 has been saved. It is peanuts. They provide for peanuts in this bill. The point that I

want to emphasize is the rapid escalation in wages in this country, not only wages of manufacturers producing goods but wages of management and executive salaries. These are all expenses added to the cost of goods and services. It is not just the man who is on the lathe whose wages have gone up, or the wages of the truck driver. It is also front-office salaries.
We have also seen tax and utility bills from the municipalities. Municipal taxes go up by fantastic amounts. Even last year municipalities increased fees by hundreds of percentage points in the belief that they were not bound by controls. Some people have lost their sense of proportion. That applies not only to those on the workbench; it applies also to government administrators at all levels in this country. Here, at the federal government level, we have departments exempting themselves from AIB guidelines. For instance, we see officials of the Ministry of Transport increasing fees to a level far in excess of any guidelines. All these increases can be seen in the increased costs. They are translated into the price of goods that we sell abroad and the price of goods we sell to our Canadian consumers. Is it any wonder that we are now finding more intense competition from suppliers abroad, imports in traditional Canadian markets, in foodstuffs, wearing apparel, manufactured goods, from distant corners of the world?
We have keener competition from the United States, from Japan and the very able manufacturing industry in Taiwan. We sit here crying in our beer about it. Every day there are delegations and trade associations which come to parliament to see the government. They want help in selling textiles, shoes, electronics or call for restrictions and quotas. We see delegations from the agricultural industry as well. I should like to see where we do not have supply management and restrictions. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is the greatest one for imposing restrictions on imports. Why is that? For example, when medium eggs in Bellingham, Washington, are selling at 66 cents, the Egg Marketing Board puts them on the market at 89 cents. Does it cost that much more in Canada to produce a dozen eggs?
We talk about Canada facing a dilemma. It is here that we are facing it. On the one hand there was the Kennedy round of some years ago which resulted in a number of reductions in tariffs. These are rates to which Canada adhered but, like a foolish virgin, we entered the league and said "Yes, we will reduce many of our customs rates." But other countries, many of them our major trading partners, particularly in Europe, resort to non-tariff barriers. So it is downright foolishness to think that we would gain by a reduction in certain rates. It is naive, because Britain, for instance, does not have to do anything; it can lower its rates on the importation of generators, something which Canadian manufacturers are well able to do. But let a Canadian manufacturer go to the electricity board in the United Kingdom to get the specifications on which to tender: the board replies that on instruction from the government, tenders are restricted to the sufficient number of British manufacturers in existence. The second change is an amendment to tariff item 69605-1 which provides free entry for a wide range of goods including scientific preparations imported by hospitals and other institutions. The provision for scientific preparations had been restricted to preparations used directly in scientific research. However, a recent Tariff Board decision had the effect of broadening the interpretation of this provision to the point where virtually all preparations used by hospitals and other institutions would be entitled to duty-free entry. Many of these preparations are available from Canadian producers. The amendment will restore the coverage of this item to that which prevailed before the Tariff Board decision. These changes came into effect on October 14, the day following the tabling of the new ways and means motion.
The principal provision of this bill will continue, until June 30, 1977, a number of the temporary reductions which were first introduced as an anti-inflationary measure in the budget of February 19, 1973, and which had been scheduled to expire on June 30 of this year. Several food products have been added to the list of items on which temporary tariff cuts were in force prior to June 30. These include fresh pork, ham, bacon, macaroni and other pasta products. In addition, deeper cuts than those previously in force have been made on certain canned meats.
I should mention, however, that tires, tubes and scissors have been dropped from the list because it was judged that the tariff reductions previously in force were causing serious problems for Canadian producers and adversely affecting employment in Canada. The tariff cuts on these products were simply allowed to expire, as previously scheduled, on June 30, 1976. If it should turn out that the temporary tariff cuts on any of the products, particularly with regard to imported meat products, that remain in the package are causing genuine hardship to Canadian producers or workers, there is authority in the bill to restore tariff protection to previous levels by order in council prior to the proposed new expiry date of June 30, 1977.
In the food sector, reductions are being continued on such products as raw and refined sugar, certain fresh and processed vegetables, a number of fish products and prepared cereal foods and biscuits. In the non-food sector, reductions are being maintained on such products as drugs and pharmaceutical products, kitchen and dinnerware, plumbing fixtures, hand-tools, photographic equipment and sporting goods. The temporary reductions proposed in this bill affect imports of consumer goods valued at about $1.6 billion in terms of 1975 imports. Close to half of these are in the food sector, about $727 million worth.
As was mentioned in the budget speech, the continuation of these temporary tariff cuts until June 30, 1977, should not prejudice our position in the multilateral trade negotiations. The reductions are temporary and they will not be the base from which we will be negotiating in Geneva. The bill also

provides for the introduction of a number of miscellaneous tariff changes. I think it would be fair to say that the most significant of these miscellaneous amendments is the introduction of tariff item 42701-1. This new item provides for the withdrawal from Britain and Ireland of the 2V4 per cent British preferential tariff on compressor sets and electricity-generating sets. Commencing on May 26, the day following the budget, the most favoured nation tariff of 15 per cent became applicable. Remission of the duty will still be allowed, however, under the machinery program in respect of any sets which are not available from Canadian production.
The tariff on this machinery is being increased because Canadian manufacturers were finding it increasingly difficult to compete against imports over the 2'h per cent tariff. A number of major contracts for this kind of machinery are expected to be let in the next few years, and the government decided that inasmuch as we are no longer obliged to accord preferential tariff rates to Britain and Ireland following their joining the European Community, the time had come to provide Canadian manufacturers of compressors and generating sets with the same level of protection against imports from these sources as they receive against imports from other countries. The study of the tariffs on other machinery which was announced in the budget speech is now well under way. Officials of the Department of Finance have solicited the views and comments of interested Canadian firms on the pros and cons of continuing the preferential rates for such machinery.
The other miscellaneous tariff changes proposed in the bill are designed to facilitate imports. They include provision for the continued duty-free entry, on a temporary basis, of aircraft and aircraft engines and of certain printing plates and irrigation equipment. A number of new tariff items are being introduced to provide free entry for such goods as low-protein and protein-free products and other special dietary foods required by persons afflicted with hereditary metabolic diseases, and-this is of particular interest to the petroleum sector-computer tapes containing seismic data. Finally, it is proposed to amend the wording of several existing tariff items either for purposes of clarification or to broaden the coverage.
This is by way of introduction of the bill. We will have an opportunity to look into the items in committee of the whole. I shall look forward to questions by members and will do my best to answer them.

speechtext: Is the Canadian Industries Limited plant in Valleyfield, Quebec, which manufactures explosives and shell fillings for the Canadian Armed Forces, closing this summer and, if so, what are the government's plans to meet this contingency?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer (Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: CIL-EXPLOSIVES AND SHELL FILLINGS
speechtext: The Canadian Industries Limited plant in Valleyfield, Quebec has been closed since late February 1976 due to strike action by process workers. The government has contracts with the Company for both propellant and explosives. At the completion of the current propellant contract, the Company has announced that it will discontinue propellant manufacture at the Valleyfield site. Unless other arrangements can be made for an alternate Canadian source, Canadian propellant requirements will be procured from outside of Canada. Procurement of explosives will continue from the CIL plant. However, should the labour dispute not be resolved in a time frame to meet our contract delivery schedules, it may be necessary to procure some of this material outside of Canada.

speechtext:
Prior to 1959, varying numbers of rail cars have been owned or on loan from Canadian National Railways and were assigned to various Ministers and Departments. During 1959, the matter of rail car use was reviewed by the Government and it was decided that the cars be reduced in number to two for the use of any Members of Cabinet, by arrangement. This recommendation was accepted with two cars being returned to CN and the remaining two (along with the 2 car unit assigned to the Governor General) put under Transport Canada's jurisdiction and assigned to the Prime Minister and Minister of Transport respectively. Four car stewards presently share the required duties as two man teams on the four rail cars and constitute the major fixed cost along with basic supplies and maintenance such as: heating, cleaning, replacement of equipment, parts, etc. Any charges from the railways for special switching, food or train requirements are charged to the user of the car. On the basis of this decision by the Government in 1959 the cars, when not in use by the assigned Ministers, have been made available on a first come-first served basis for foreign dignitaries, Members of Cabinet and senior officials of the Canadian Transport Commission. Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railways issue passes for Ministers authorizing use of the rail car plus the two attendants. Any other persons on the cars are charged by the railway for first class passage (unless they hold railway passes in their own right). As with the CN and CP passes issued to Members of Parliament, the purpose of the trip has never been requested and Members and Ministers may exercise the use of their passes for whatever purpose they choose. Other than the first class charge for any passengers, the railways have traditionally hauled the four rail cars at no cost on regular train operations. This means that with most of the costs being of a fixed nature, there is very little difference in cost whether the cars are in use or on standby. The fact that accommodation and meeting rooms are not required is an additional incentive to use the cars rather than commercial facilities. It is necessary to maintain this small number of rail cars in Ottawa in any case for matters of state and the use therefore, by
Order Paper Questions
approved officials, becomes an efficient use of facilities that are already paid for. There is periodic assessment of the feasibility of hiring rail car stewards from the railway as required rather than paying annual salaries and to date it has been considerably more economical to pay annual salaries. The rail cars allow the necessary privacy required for working conditions while travelling and allow maintenance of the level of security needed for the Prime Minister and for foreign dignitaries (see page 8618 of Hansard for December 11, 1973). In addition to the security features and controlled working environment, there has traditionally been, in the use of these cars by the Government's most senior representatives, the recognition of their need to travel to various parts of the country as part of their responsibilities. The cars have never been restricted to any specific use other than during general election campaigns.
